name: High Tory
summary: High Toryism is the old traditionalist wing of British Toryism. As the sources present it in the 1830s, it favoured a hierarchical, paternalist society over freedom and equality, saw the state as an organic body rooted in the past, held the Established Church and state inseparable ('Church in Danger'), held property sacred and resisted reform, against the more pragmatic Liberal Tories.
scope: High Toryism as the sources present it: the old, hierarchical, paternalist and High Church Anglican strand of Toryism that rallied to 'Church in Danger' from Queen Anne's time and, in the 1830s, under Eldon and Sidmouth, defended the established church and constitution and resisted reform, in contrast to the 'liberal' Tories (Canning, Huskisson, Peel). The sources also give the Burkean view of the state as an organic body rooted in the past. It excludes liberal Toryism, One-Nation reformism and Thatcherite neoliberalism.
notes: Only two defining sources outside Wikipedia name High Toryism, both about the early nineteenth century; most statements are null. Themes searched: church and state, hierarchy and equality, property, reform, monarchy, free trade. Free trade is null: the thesis says it wasn't an ideological dividing line for High Tories before the 1840s. Positions the essay gives only for Gladstone, not for High Tories generally, are null.
